concepts.name: Unparalleled Realism
concepts.description: Convolution reverb uses impulse responses captured from real spaces or devices. When you load an IR of a grand cathedral or iconic studio chamber, you’re hearing that exact acoustic fingerprint. The resulting _realism_ is often unmatched, making convolution reverb ideal for classical recordings, film scoring, and any situation where a lifelike environment is essential.

concepts.name: Authentic Character
concepts.description: Different rooms have distinct tonal imprints. A large concert hall may emphasize certain [midrange frequencies](https://www.soundonsound.com/glossary/mid-range-mid-mids) while rolling off highs over time. An underground bunker might produce a darker, more ominous decay. Convolution reverb preserves these unique acoustic nuances, allowing you to “place” sounds in specific, evocative environments.

concepts.name: High CPU Usage
concepts.description: Convolution involves complex math to multiply your audio by the impulse response. Longer IRs and higher sample rates require more processing power. If you’re layering multiple convolution reverbs across numerous tracks, your CPU might struggle. Some users circumvent this by placing just one convolution reverb on an aux bus, then sending multiple instruments to it.

concepts.name: Limited Flexibility
concepts.description: Because impulse responses are essentially fixed snapshots, extreme changes in decay time or room size can sound unnatural. You can usually adjust pre-delay, EQ, or overall decay trimming, but truly reshaping the space is trickier. If you need a radically different reverb tail, you might have to swap IRs or rely on specialized stretching techniques.

concepts.name: Creative Control
concepts.description: Algorithmic reverb is engineered from scratch. Designers assemble delay networks, feedback paths, and filters into a system that simulates reflections. In many plugins, you can tweak decay time, room size, diffusion, and modulation to shape the reverb in imaginative ways. Want a 30-second tail that evolves and shimmers? You can dial that in with a few slider movements.

concepts.name: Lower CPU Demand
concepts.description: Algorithmic reverbs generally require fewer resources. You can often run multiple instances without overwhelming your system. If you have a dense session with many tracks, algorithmic reverb can be a lifesaver.

concepts.name: Can Sound Artificial
concepts.description: Older or poorly designed algorithms might exhibit ringing or metallic resonances. While modern algorithmic reverbs have improved significantly, achieving a smooth, natural decay still hinges on solid engineering. If you’re aiming for absolute _realism_, algorithmic approaches sometimes fall short—though high-end plugins can blur that line.

concepts.name: Not a Perfect Acoustic Match
concepts.description: If you want to replicate a specific real-world venue, algorithmic reverb won’t capture it perfectly. It can approximate many environments, but for a truly faithful reproduction of a famous church or recording studio, convolution is generally superior.

concepts.name: Convolution Reverb
concepts.description: Tends to be heavier on CPU, especially with long or detailed IRs. Latency might arise if the plugin uses partitioned convolution with certain buffering modes, but many plugins now offer near-zero-latency processing at the cost of extra CPU cycles.

concepts.name: Algorithmic Reverb
concepts.description: Generally lighter on CPU, allowing many instances without hitting performance limits. Latency is often minimal or zero, making it a great choice if you’re tracking live instruments and need immediate feedback from your effects.

concepts.name: Realistic Spaces
concepts.description: If you’re mixing a small jazz combo and you want them to sound like they’re performing in a famous club, convolution reverb delivers that authentic vibe. It’s also excellent for orchestral or chamber recordings, where the natural resonance of a concert hall adds grandeur.

concepts.name: Film and Dialogue
concepts.description: For film, TV, or game audio where matching the on-screen environment is essential, convolution reverb is a fast and straightforward solution. You can dial up a church, tunnel, or living room IR, giving your sounds the appropriate reverberant fingerprint.

concepts.name: Hardware Emulations
concepts.description: Some convolution plugins let you load impulse responses of vintage gear, like classic plates or spring reverb units. If you want the distinct coloration of a legendary hardware unit, convolution can come surprisingly close to the real hardware’s character.

concepts.name: Creative Sound Design
concepts.description: Algorithmic reverbs let you push boundaries. From otherworldly shimmer tails to pitch-shifted reflections, you can craft unique ambiences well beyond any natural space.

concepts.name: Efficiency
concepts.description: If your session is massive and you need multiple reverbs running smoothly, algorithmic reverb is generally more CPU-friendly. You can fine-tune decay, diffusion, and tonal shaping without adding significant load.

concepts.name: Pop, Rock, and Electronic Mixing
concepts.description: Modern vocal mixes often rely on algorithmic reverbs for that signature sheen. Drums in rock or electronic tracks might need bright, snappy rooms or huge, modulated halls. Algorithmic reverbs are built for this kind of everyday mix shaping.

concepts.name: Delay lines.
concepts.description: A “delay line” allows you to read from and write to a memory buffer and increment through that buffer every sample. The distance between your read and write points determines how much the signal is delayed from the input to the output. An algorithmic reverb will have several to several dozen of these, all at different delay lengths.

concepts.name: Filters.
concepts.description: A digital filter is used to control the high and/or low-frequency balance of a signal. In a digital reverb, filters are often placed in the feedback path of a delay, where the signal is filtered, scaled by a value, and added back into the input.

concepts.name: Modulators.
concepts.description: Many digital reverbs (including all of the Valhalla reverbs) will slowly vary the delay lengths over time. This requires fractional delays that use linear or higher-order interpolation, but that’s a concept beyond this introduction. The important point is that you need some sort of modulator to vary things slowly. These are often low-frequency oscillators or some sort of band-limited noise.

concepts.name: Add/subtract/multiply.
concepts.description: These are the building blocks for creating feedback around the delays, as well as feeding a signal around a delay (as found in allpass delays), scaling the outputs of the reverb, and creating matrices for mixing signals together before they are fed back into the inputs, stuff like that.

concepts.name: Convolution
concepts.description: for the cohesive, natural ambience.

concepts.name: Algorithmic
concepts.description: for sculpted tails or special effects.

Years back, Matsushita/Panasonic came up with a multi-tap bucket-brigade chip, the MN3011, that was intended to provide "solid-state reverb". The 6 taps were at mathematically unrelated numbers of stages such that there would be no accidental creation of unwanted resonances. Sounded great in theory, but the chip ended up being a bit of a dog and was discontinued. Why? The few schematics I've been able to see, for reverb pedals that used the chip, neglected one important factor in mimicking natural reverb: the fact that simple amplitude and number of reflections/repeats will not get you a "natural" sound. There was NO differential filtering of early and late reflections. Heck, there usually wasn't even a global Tone control for the wet signal. Natural reverberant spaces are not just polished marble walls or glass. There are absorbant surfaces, furniture, people, and other objects in the way and the usual sound shadow that happens when a reflection from point X reaches one ear earlier than the re-reflection that has to bounce off another surface before arriving at the other ear.
